candidates.source_name: Cyril of Alexandria / Commentary on Luke
candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXVI (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's cleansing of the Temple — 'It is written, My house is the house of prayer: but ye have made it a den of thieves' (Lk 19:46) — Cyril reads the citation of Isa 56:7 + Jer 7:11 as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine that the consecrated-place is by-definition the house-of-prayer; commerce within the precinct DEFILES the consecration. Christ's action is canonical-prophetic, not anti-Temple in principle (Christ continues to teach there daily, Lk 19:47). Tewahedo church-discipline cites Lk 19:46 + Is 56:7 + Jer 7:11 as the canonical triple-witness that the church-building is by definition the house-of-prayer; commercial use of the precinct (vending, money-changing) is excluded by canonical prophet-and-dominical authority.

candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's call to Zacchaeus 'make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house' (Lk 19:5), Cyril reads the dei-me (it-is-necessary-for-me) as the canonical Lukan anchor of the doctrine of Christ's seeking-grace: the dominical 'I must lodge with thee' is a divine-imperative, not a guest's-request. Christ initiates the encounter; Zacchaeus's tree-climbing met halfway by Christ's calling-down. Tewahedo evangelism-theology cites Lk 19:5 + Lk 19:10 (Son of Man come to seek-and-save) as the canonical Lukan doubled-witness of the doctrine that Christ initiates the salvation-encounter; the priestly-pastor follows the dominical-pattern of seeking-the-Zacchaeuses.

Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

'This day is salvation come to this house' — Cyril reads the Zacchaeus pericope as the canonical Lukan diptych to Lk 15: in Lk 15 the lost son returns to the father; in Lk 19 the lost son is sought-and-found by the Father. The Son of Man came TO SEEK AND TO SAVE — the seeking is the divine initiative. Tewahedo missiology cites Lk 19:10 alongside Lk 15:20 as the canonical seeking-and-running diptych.

candidates.source_name: Cyril of Alexandria / Commentary on Luke
candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXVII (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Lk 5:32.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On Christ's mission-statement at the Zacchaeus episode 'For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost' (Lk 19:10), Cyril reads the doubled-mission (seek + save) as the canonical Lukan summary-statement of the Incarnation's purpose: the Son of Man's earthly trajectory (already-emphasized at Lk 5:32 — come to call sinners) reaches its compact-definitive expression here. The verse becomes load-bearing for the patristic doctrine of the missio Dei — God's outgoing mission preceding any human response. Tewahedo missionary theology cites Lk 19:10 + Lk 5:32 as the canonical Lukan doubled-witness of the doctrine that Christian mission participates in the dominical-search-and-rescue mission; the Tewahedo apostolic-outreach to the Beta-Israel and surrounding peoples is the appropriation of this canonical pattern.

candidates.source_name: Cyril of Alexandria / Commentary on Luke
candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXIX (R. Payne Smith trans., 1859). PD. Cf. Lk 2:14. Tewahedo liturgical witness: Hosanna feast.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

On the triumphal-entry cry 'Blessed be the King that cometh in the name of the Lord: peace in heaven, and glory in the highest' (Lk 19:38), Cyril reads the Lukan-distinctive 'peace in heaven' (where the Synoptic parallels say 'Hosanna in the highest') as the canonical Lukan anchor of the cosmic-reconciliation announcement: heaven-and-earth peace is the explicit content of Christ's triumphal-entry. The phrase echoes the angelic Christmas-hymn (Lk 2:14 — peace-on-earth) and now reverses: peace-on-earth then, peace-in-heaven now. Tewahedo Hosanna-procession (Hosanna feast — the Sunday before Pascha) cites Lk 19:38 alongside Lk 2:14 as the canonical Lukan-doubled-witness of the peace-of-the-incarnation completed at the Cross.

candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on Luke, Homily CXXVIII (R. Payne Smith trans., Oxford: University Press, 1859). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on Luke (c. 430 AD)

Christ's weeping over Jerusalem is for Cyril the canonical disclosure of the Lord's mercy precisely toward the city about to reject him. The tears do not soften the prophetic announcement of the city's destruction; they intensify it as the announcement of a real and grievous loss. Cyril rejects every reading that would treat the tears as mere stagecraft. Tewahedo Holy-Week lectionary preserves Lk 19:41-44 as the Palm-Sunday-eve reading of the Lord's lament.
